title: Does a ramp save you work?
hook: A long ramp makes a heavy crate easy to push. So it must save effort. Does it?

knows: ramps make lifting heavy things easier
force in newtons; weight is mass x 9.81
doesNotKnow: that the force saved by a ramp is paid for in distance

misconception: A ramp reduces the work needed to raise a load.
objective: The learner can explain that a longer frictionless ramp needs a smaller push (m g h / L) over a longer path, so the work, force x distance, stays m g h: 122.6 N x 4 m = 490.5 J for 50 kg raised 1 m.

claims.text: On a frictionless ramp, the steady push needed along the slope is weight x height / length (m g sin theta).
claims.source: Resolve weight along the incline: m g sin(theta), with sin(theta) = h / L; at constant speed the push balances it. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 5-6.

claims.text: Raising 50 kg by 1.0 m along a 4 m frictionless ramp takes the same work as lifting it straight up: a push of 122.6 N × 4 m = 490.5 J against 490.5 N × 1 m = 490.5 J (the stage log shows each finished push as push × length = work, to 0.1 N).
claims.source: 50 x 9.81 x 1 / 4 = 122.6 N; x 4 m = 490.5 J = m g h. The stage computes 490.5 / L for L = 1-8 m (490.5, 245.3, 163.5, 122.6, 98.1, 81.8, 70.1, 61.3 N); checked in node. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check.

claims.text: Work is force x distance moved along the force, so a smaller push over a longer path does the same work.
claims.source: W = F d for a constant force parallel to the motion; (m g h / L) x L = m g h. Work-energy theorem, Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 7.

claims.text: The lesson assumes no friction and a steady (constant-speed) push; real ramps add friction work, so they cost a little more work, not less.
claims.source: Stated on stage ('Frictionless. Steady push.') and in the reveal. With kinetic friction mu, extra work mu m g cos(theta) L is added.

claims.text: A 50 kg crate weighs about 490 N (50 kg × 9.81 m/s²).
claims.source: Weight = m g with g = 9.81 m/s²; 50 × 9.81 = 490.5 N. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): 50 x 9.81 = 490.5 N (Demo.tsx G = 9.81, M = 50); with standard gravity 9.80665 m/s^2 (CGPM 1901) it is 490.3 N; 'about 490 N' holds either way. Predict text matches.

recall.question: Two ramps lift the same box onto the same truck bed: one 2 m long, one 6 m long, both frictionless. Which needs more work?
recall.why: The longer ramp needs a third of the push over three times the distance; work = force x distance = m g h either way.
